Let <MATH_0001> be a diagram. In this setting a
<TEXTITOPEN_0001>cone<TEXTITCLOSE_0001> for <MATH_0002> is given by an object <MATH_0003> and a family of morphisms
<MATH_0004>, <MATH_0005> such that for all morphisms
<MATH_0006> of <MATH_0007> the diagram
<MATH_0008>
is commutative. The collection of cones forms a category with an obvious
notion of morphisms. Clearly, the limit of <MATH_0009>, if it exists, is a final
object in the category of cones. Dually, a <TEXTITOPEN_0002>cocone<TEXTITCLOSE_0002> for <MATH_0010> is given
by an object <MATH_0011> and a family of morphisms <MATH_0012> such that for
all morphisms <MATH_0013> in <MATH_0014> the diagram
<MATH_0015>
commutes. The collection of cocones forms a category with an obvious notion
of morphisms. Similarly to the above the colimit of <MATH_0016> exists
if and only if the category of cocones has an initial object.
